lessons.title: What is the Grundrisse?
lessons.eyebrow: Start here · no prior reading needed
lessons.description: Meet the manuscript: eight notebooks written in a crisis winter, published eighty years later, and read ever since as Marx’s workshop.
objectives: Place the Grundrisse between the 1844 Manuscripts and Capital
Explain why it was unknown until the twentieth century
Read a rough draft for its arguments rather than its polish

sections.heading: A manuscript written against the clock
paragraphs: In the autumn of 1857 a commercial crisis spread from New York to Britain and the continent. Marx, living in London and earning his keep as a newspaper correspondent, expected the slump to reopen the revolutionary period of 1848. He wanted his critique of political economy in order before it did, and wrote through the nights from August 1857 into the spring of 1858.

The result was an Introduction in a notebook he labelled ‘M’ and seven numbered notebooks—roughly eight hundred printed pages—written for self-clarification, not for readers. The title by which we know them was given by later editors: Grundrisse der Kritik der politischen Ökonomie (Rohentwurf), ‘Outlines of the Critique of Political Economy (Rough Draft)’.

sections.heading: Between Hegel and Capital
paragraphs: The notebooks are where Marx first works out the theory of surplus value and the distinction between the exchange of equivalents and the use of labour. Their vocabulary is openly dialectical—moments, positing, presuppositions, contradictions—and some terms are still in motion: the worker sells ‘labour’ or ‘labour capacity’ here, ‘labour-power’ in Capital.

Only a small part reached print in Marx’s lifetime, reworked as A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy (1859). The full manuscript was published in Moscow in 1939 and 1941, barely circulated during the war, and became widely available with a Berlin edition in 1953. Martin Nicolaus’s complete English translation appeared in 1973.
sections.callout: The Grundrisse is a laboratory, not a textbook: you watch the categories being tested.

sections.heading: How to read a rough draft
paragraphs: Expect repetition, long digressions, notes to self, and passages that stop mid-thought. Read for movements of argument rather than for definitions: ask where a category comes from, what problem it is solving, and where it breaks down. Many sections reappear several hundred pages later in improved form.

This course follows the manuscript’s order but selects its strongest threads. Every lesson cites the page numbers of the Penguin edition, which the online text marks as anchors, so you can always step from the guide into Marx’s own sequence.

example.title: Follow one thread: time
example.body: Time runs through the whole manuscript. Money is objectified labour time (p. 168); all economy reduces to economy of time (p. 173); surplus value is surplus labour time (p. 321); circulation time is time of devaluation (p. 537); and the Fragment on Machines ends with disposable time (p. 708). Tracking one thread like this is the best way into the notebooks.

lessons.distinction: Avoid two shortcuts: treating the Grundrisse as the ‘real’ Marx hidden behind Capital, or as a discarded draft Capital made redundant. It is a stage of research—some ideas were refined later, some were dropped, and some appear nowhere else.

quiz.question: Why is the Grundrisse called a ‘rough draft’?
options: It is an abridgement of Capital prepared by Engels
Marx wrote it in notebooks to clarify his own thinking, not for publication
It collects newspaper articles from the 1857 crisis
It is a set of notes taken at Marx’s lectures
quiz.explanation: The notebooks were research for self-clarification; editors gave them the subtitle Rohentwurf, ‘rough draft’.

quiz.question: When was the complete manuscript first published?
quiz.explanation: The German original appeared in Moscow in 1939 and 1941; the full English translation followed in 1973.

lessons.title: Production in general
lessons.description: Why Marx refuses to start from an isolated individual, what makes an abstraction ‘rational’, and how production, distribution, exchange and consumption form one whole.
objectives: Explain the critique of ‘Robinsonades’
Distinguish a rational abstraction from an eternalizing one
Describe production, distribution, exchange and consumption as moments of a totality

sections.heading: Against the Robinsonades
paragraphs: Smith and Ricardo began from a solitary hunter or fisherman, a Robinson Crusoe exchanging with others by nature. Marx answers that this self-sufficient individual is not where history starts but what eighteenth-century civil society produced. The further back we go, the more the individual appears as a dependent member of a larger whole: family, clan, community.

Humans, he says borrowing Aristotle, are political animals—beings who can only individuate themselves within society. Production by an isolated individual outside society is as unlikely as the development of a language without people living and talking together.

sections.heading: A rational abstraction
paragraphs: Every epoch of production shares some features: there is always a subject (humanity) and an object (nature), always instruments and past labour. ‘Production in general’ is a legitimate abstraction insofar as it fixes these common elements and spares repetition.

The danger is to let the common elements swallow the differences. Economists like J. S. Mill argued that because no production happens without instruments and stored labour, capital is an eternal condition of production. Marx’s rule is the reverse: the essential thing is the specific difference that makes production in a given epoch what it is.
sections.callout: An abstraction is rational when it saves repetition—and misleading when it erases history.

sections.heading: One whole, four moments
paragraphs: Political economy arranged production, distribution, exchange and consumption as a neat syllogism: production general, distribution and exchange particular, consumption individual. Marx shows instead that each is internally linked to the others. Production consumes raw materials and labour; consumption produces the consumer and creates the need that production answers; production supplies not only an object but a way of consuming it.

Distribution is not an independent sphere of fairness or unfairness. Before products are distributed, the instruments of production and the members of society have already been distributed among kinds of production. Production therefore predominates, though all four moments act on one another as in any organic whole.

example.title: A café, four ways
example.body: Brewing coffee consumes beans, machines and hours of work. Drinking it reproduces a customer who comes back tomorrow. Exchange moves cups for money. But who receives wages and who receives profit was settled earlier—by who owns the café and who must work in it. Distribution of products follows the distribution of the means of production.

lessons.distinction: ‘Production predominates’ is not technological determinism. Marx insists the moments interact; his target is the separation of a ‘natural’ sphere of production from a ‘historical’ sphere of distribution.

quiz.question: What does Marx object to in the ‘Robinsonade’ starting point?
options: It uses fictional examples at all
It ignores the role of barter
It treats the isolated individual—a historical product—as the natural starting point
It overstates the importance of agriculture
quiz.explanation: The independent individual is a result of modern civil society, not a timeless premise.

quiz.question: According to the Introduction, the distribution of products presupposes…
options: a fair wage set by law
the prior distribution of instruments of production and of people among branches of production
quiz.explanation: Who gets what share of output depends on who owns the means of production and who works in which branch.

lessons.title: Rising from the abstract to the concrete
lessons.description: Marx’s most explicit statement of method: why ‘population’ is a poor starting point, why categories are not ordered by history, and the puzzle of Greek art.
objectives: Describe the two paths between abstract and concrete
Explain why the order of categories follows modern society, not chronology
State the problem of uneven development raised by Greek art

sections.heading: Two paths
paragraphs: It seems right to start with something real and concrete, such as a country’s population. But population is an empty abstraction if we leave out the classes it consists of; classes mean nothing without wage labour and capital; these presuppose exchange, division of labour and prices. Starting with the whole gives only a chaotic picture.

The seventeenth-century economists travelled from that chaotic whole down to a few thin determinations—labour, division of labour, need, exchange value. The scientifically correct path is the return journey: from simple determinations back up to the state, international exchange and the world market. The concrete then reappears as a rich totality of many determinations and relations.
sections.callout: In thought the concrete arrives at the end—as a result gathering many determinations—even though in reality it is the starting point.

sections.heading: Not Hegel, not chronology
paragraphs: Hegel, Marx says, mistook this movement of thought for the process by which the concrete itself comes into being. For Marx the rising method is only how thinking appropriates a reality that exists independently outside the head.

Nor should the categories follow their order of historical appearance. Simple categories such as money can exist before developed ones such as capital, yet they reach full development only in modern society. Even ‘labour’ as such—labour in general, indifferent to its particular kind—became a practical truth only where people move easily between jobs. Hence the image that human anatomy holds a key to the anatomy of the ape: the developed form illuminates earlier ones, as long as differences are not blurred. Capital, not landed property, must therefore come first in the presentation.

sections.heading: Greek art and uneven development
paragraphs: Section 4 is a list of notes, but one is developed: the relation between material production and art is uneven. Greek art rested on a mythology that becomes impossible alongside railways, telegraphs and lightning conductors.

The hard question, Marx says, is not explaining why Greek epic arose in its society but why it still gives us aesthetic pleasure and counts in some respects as an unattainable model. His tentative answer—its charm as the art of humanity’s historical childhood—matters less than the warning: the link between production and culture is not mechanical.

example.title: From a phone’s price to the world market
example.body: A smartphone’s price is the chaotic concrete. Analysis breaks it into value, money, wages, profit, rent and taxes. Presentation then rebuilds it—through capital, competition, credit, the state and global supply chains—until the price reappears as the concentration of all those relations.

lessons.distinction: The method of presentation is not the method of research. Marx studied the concrete first; he presents from the simplest categories. And the rising method does not mean thought creates reality—that is exactly his objection to Hegel.

source.label: Introduction §3 · The method of political economy (p. 100)

furtherReading.label: Introduction §4 · Production, relations of production, art (p. 109)

quiz.question: Why is ‘population’ a misleading place to start?
options: Population belongs to biology, not economics
It is an abstraction until classes, wage labour, capital and exchange are understood
quiz.explanation: The apparently concrete whole is empty until the simpler relations that compose it have been grasped.

quiz.question: What problem does Marx raise about Greek art?
options: Why it can still give pleasure and serve as a model after its social basis has vanished
quiz.explanation: Explaining its origin is easy; explaining its lasting appeal shows that art and production develop unevenly.

lessons.title: Darimon and the dream of labour-money
lessons.description: Marx opens the notebooks by taking apart a Proudhonist plan to abolish crises through bank reform and ‘time-chits’—and discovers why money cannot simply be decreed away.
objectives: Summarize Darimon’s proposal and Marx’s objection
Explain why value and price must diverge
Show why an hour-note cannot keep representing an hour

sections.heading: A bank reform to abolish crises?
paragraphs: Alfred Darimon, a follower of Proudhon, argued in 1856 that crises came from the privileged position of gold and silver and the policy of the Bank of France. Reform the instrument of circulation—free credit, notes not tied to metal—and the crises would disappear.

Marx begins by checking Darimon’s own Bank of France figures and finds them misread. Then he poses the real question: can a change in the instrument of circulation revolutionize the relations of production and distribution? His answer runs through the whole chapter: the contradictions of money are the contradictions of exchange value itself, and they reappear in any money that private exchange requires.

sections.heading: Time-chits
paragraphs: A more radical version, associated with Gray, Bray and the Proudhonists, would replace gold with notes certifying hours of labour. Marx’s objection is that a commodity’s value is set not by the labour time it actually took but by the labour time currently necessary to reproduce it. As productivity changes, an hour embodied yesterday is no longer worth an hour today.

The note would then have to depreciate or appreciate against goods—so it would no longer be an hour—or the issuing bank would have to buy and sell everything at fixed rates and thereby become the despotic manager of all production. Value exists only as an average that asserts itself through constant deviations of price; a time-chit treats that average as if it could be paid out directly.
sections.callout: Value is not a label stuck on a product. It is a social average that only shows itself through prices that never quite match it.

sections.heading: Why money arises
paragraphs: Every commodity leads a double life: as a useful thing and as exchange value. For private producers to compare their products, exchange value must take on an existence separate from all of them—first in thought, then in a special commodity. That separate existence is money.

Money is therefore not a technical convenience that could be abolished while private exchange continues. Reforming money while keeping commodity production leaves the source of its contradictions intact.

example.title: An hour-note in a productivity boom
example.body: A coat takes 10 hours, so the bank prices it at 10 hour-notes. New machines cut the time to 5 hours. Either the coat now sells for 5 notes—and notes no longer measure the labour actually spent—or the bank keeps the 10-note price and sits on unsaleable coats. Try it in the Time-chit lab.

lessons.distinction: Marx does not reject allocating labour time by plan in a society without commodity exchange—he discusses exactly that at p. 172. His target is reforming money while keeping private exchange.

source.label: Chapter on Money · Darimon’s theory of crises (p. 115)

quiz.question: What is Marx’s central objection to Darimon?
options: Gold is the natural measure of value
Bank reform cannot remove contradictions rooted in exchange value and private production
Crises are caused by high wages
quiz.explanation: Changing the form of money leaves untouched the exchange relations that generate money’s contradictions.

quiz.question: Why can’t an hour-note stay equal to an hour’s worth of goods?
options: Because value follows currently necessary labour time, which changes with productivity
Because chits cannot be printed fast enough
quiz.explanation: Past hours embodied in a product count only as the hours now socially necessary to reproduce it.

lessons.title: Money as social bond
lessons.description: Marx’s sketch of three great social forms—personal dependence, objective dependence, free individuality—and the ‘economy of time’ that would replace value.
objectives: Explain how money carries social power ‘in the pocket’
Describe the three social forms and how they relate
Distinguish planned economy of time from value

sections.heading: Power in the pocket
paragraphs: In a developed exchange society, everyone produces for everyone else, yet each pursues only private interest. Their mutual dependence takes the form of an alien, objective relation—exchange value—standing outside and above them. The individual carries social power, and the bond with society, in a pocket: as money.

Private interest, Marx stresses, is already socially determined. What one can pursue and by what means is set by conditions the society provides; the market is not a natural arena that private wills happen to meet in.

sections.heading: Three great social forms
paragraphs: Marx compresses history into three forms (p. 158). First, relations of personal dependence, at first entirely natural, in which human productivity develops only narrowly and at isolated points. Second, personal independence founded on objective dependence: a general metabolism of social exchange, universal relations, all-round needs and capacities. Third, free individuality based on the universal development of individuals and on their common, social productivity mastered as their own wealth.

The second form creates the conditions of the third. That rules out both romantic longing for an original fullness and the bourgeois belief that history stops at the second stage. Individuals are now ruled by abstractions, where earlier they depended on one another—but the abstractions express real relations that could be brought under common control.
sections.callout: Personal freedom from a lord; objective dependence on a price.

sections.heading: The economy of time
paragraphs: If production were communal, time would still matter. Society would have to divide its labour time among branches to meet its needs, and saving time would be the first economic law—all economy, Marx says, reduces itself to economy of time (pp. 172–3).

But this is essentially different from measuring exchange values by labour time. In commodity exchange, private labour becomes social only after the fact, when its product is sold. In communal production labour would be social from the outset, and its share in the product would not be mediated by the exchange of values.

example.title: A manor and a payment app
example.body: A serf owed dues to a known lord and could be punished by him in person. A gig worker owes no one personally and can log off at will—yet depends for survival on prices set by millions of strangers. Personal independence, objective dependence.

lessons.distinction: The three forms are not a strict timetable for every society. They are a schema of how social bonds can be organized, and ‘free individuality’ is a projected possibility, not a description of an existing society.

quiz.question: In the second great social form, individuals are…
options: personally dependent on a lord or community
free individuals controlling their social productivity
personally independent but dependent on objective relations such as money
quiz.explanation: Personal independence rests on dependence on things—exchange value and money.

quiz.question: How does a communal ‘economy of time’ differ from value?
options: It doesn’t—both measure exchange values by labour time
Labour is social from the start and time is allocated by plan, not through the exchange of values
It abolishes any concern with time
Value is just planning by the state
quiz.explanation: Time remains a measure of effort, but social labour is no longer validated only after the fact by sale.

lessons.title: Money’s three functions
lessons.description: Measure, medium of circulation, and money as money: how the third function—money as independent wealth—already points toward capital.
objectives: Distinguish money as measure, as medium and as money
Explain the hoarder’s paradox
Describe money as the ‘real community’

sections.heading: Measure and medium
paragraphs: As measure, money works only in the imagination: a price tag is ideal money, and no gold needs to be present for goods to be compared. As medium of circulation, in the sequence commodity–money–commodity, money is a vanishing intermediary that can be replaced by tokens and paper, because it only has to last for the moment of exchange.
The quantity of money needed for circulation depends on the sum of prices and the velocity of circulation—not the other way round, as the currency theorists believed.

sections.heading: Money as money
paragraphs: In its third function money steps out of circulation as the independent, material representative of wealth: treasure, universal means of payment, world money. Here it must be real money, because it embodies wealth in general.

This creates the hoarder’s paradox. Qualitatively, money is wealth without limit—it can buy anything. Quantitatively, every sum is limited. The drive to hold abstract wealth is therefore endless, yet the hoarder can satisfy it only by withdrawing money from circulation, where it does not grow. The way out is to throw money back into circulation in order to make it return larger: capital.
sections.callout: A hoard tries to keep value by stopping it; capital keeps value by keeping it moving.

sections.heading: Money as the community
paragraphs: Where money is not itself the community, Marx argues, it must dissolve the community (p. 223). Ancient writers already treated money’s growth as corrosive of the old order.

Once money becomes the universal means of livelihood, it is itself the real community: the general substance of everyone’s survival and the social product of all, standing over each person as an external power.

example.title: Why a hoard keeps growing
example.body: A merchant who has saved a thousand pounds is richer than one with a hundred, but both are poorer than wealth as such. Any sum can be outbid by a larger one. The only way to make a sum increase is to risk it in purchase and sale—to turn it into capital.

lessons.distinction: Hoards are not yet capital. Hoarding withdraws money from circulation; capital must keep throwing it back in. The Grundrisse’s transition to capital begins from exactly this tension.

quiz.question: In which function can money most easily be replaced by tokens?
options: As medium of circulation, where it is a fleeting intermediary
As the material of contracts settled in bullion
quiz.explanation: In C–M–C money only needs to last for the moment of exchange, so symbols can stand in for it.

quiz.question: Why does hoarding point beyond itself toward capital?
options: Wealth in general is limitless but every sum is limited, and withdrawal cannot make a sum grow
quiz.explanation: Only by re-entering circulation to return enlarged can money pursue the limitless wealth it represents.

lessons.title: Freedom, equality, and exchange
lessons.description: Why simple exchange really does produce freedom and equality—and why that is only the surface of bourgeois society.
objectives: Explain why exchangers appear free and equal
Describe circulation as a surface process
State Marx’s critique of socialists who appeal to exchange ideals

sections.heading: The exchangers’ world
paragraphs: In simple exchange the parties meet as equals: each owns an equivalent, and the difference between their needs and products is precisely what connects them. Each serves the other in order to serve himself. Nobody takes by force; property seems to rest on one’s own labour.
Marx takes this seriously. The exchange of exchange values, he writes (p. 245), is the productive, real basis of all equality and freedom; the legal forms of contract and person grow out of it.

sections.heading: A surface process
paragraphs: Yet simple circulation is only the surface of bourgeois society, behind which deeper processes go on. Already the compulsion to produce for exchange is a social one: individuals are free from personal masters, not from the market.
When the analysis moves from circulation to production, the same equality and freedom turn into inequality and unfreedom—without any exchange being broken. That is what the next lessons show.
sections.callout: Freedom and equality are real at the counter. Ask what happens behind it.

sections.heading: Against harmonizers and socialists
paragraphs: Bastiat drew from exchange a picture of universal harmony. The French socialists around Proudhon drew the opposite conclusion: society had betrayed the ideals of 1789, and socialism would finally realize freedom and equality.

Marx calls this a pious wish. The system of exchange values, once developed, becomes a system of inequality and unfreedom by its own logic. The ideals are not a broken promise to be kept, but the self-image of a mode of production whose basis contradicts them.

example.title: The employment contract
example.body: Employer and worker sign as legal equals; either may refuse. But one owns the business and the other owns only an ability to work and needs to eat this month. No personal coercion is needed; the compulsion lies in the situation each brings to the table.

lessons.distinction: Marx does not call the freedom and equality of exchange mere illusions. They are real at the level of circulation; the point is that they are partial and turn into their opposite once production is examined.

quiz.question: For Marx, the freedom and equality of simple exchange are…
options: real at the level of circulation, but a surface beneath which production works differently
the complete truth of capitalist society
quiz.explanation: They are genuinely produced by exchange of equivalents—and become their opposite in production.

quiz.question: What does Marx criticize in the French socialists?
options: Their support for the gold standard
Their wish to realize the ideals of exchange against the very system that produces them
quiz.explanation: Appealing to freedom and equality of exchange misses that the developed exchange system itself generates inequality.

lessons.title: Capital is not a thing
lessons.description: Why ‘accumulated labour’ and ‘a sum of values’ fail as definitions, why circulation cannot renew itself, and what use value capital must buy.
objectives: Criticize eternalizing definitions of capital
Explain why circulation presupposes production
Define productive labour in the Grundrisse’s sense

sections.heading: More than a sum of values
paragraphs: Economists defined capital as accumulated labour, or as a sum of values used to produce more values. On those definitions, Marx remarks, the stone in a hunter’s hand would be capital, and capital would exist wherever humans have tools.

Capital is a definite social relation of production. It is value that relates to itself as value: it preserves itself through circulation and multiplies itself. It consists of things—money, raw materials, machines—but these are capital only in a specific social setting.

sections.heading: Circulation cannot carry its own renewal
paragraphs: Simple circulation does not reproduce itself. Commodities fall out of it into consumption; money that comes to rest falls out as hoard. Circulation always presupposes something outside it that keeps throwing commodities in.

Merchant and usurer capital existed long before capitalism, but they took existing production as given and lived off its exchanges. For exchange value to perpetuate and increase itself, it must enter production and buy the thing that produces value.

sections.heading: Money meets its use value
paragraphs: The only use value that can confront capital as its opposite and enlarge it is labour itself—not labour already objectified in products, but living, value-creating labour. Capital’s use value, in this sense, is labour.

That gives Marx his definition of productive labour: labour that produces capital. A tailor who comes to your house to mend your trousers is paid out of revenue for a service consumed; the same tailor employed by a clothing firm is exchanged against capital to make it grow. The work is identical; the social form differs.
sections.callout: Same stitch, different relation: revenue buys a service, capital buys growth.

example.title: Two ways to pay a tailor
example.body: You pay a tailor 40 to hem a suit: the money is spent, the service consumed, nothing returns. A firm pays the same tailor 40 a day, sells what she makes for 60, and pays her again tomorrow. Only the second payment is an advance of capital.

lessons.distinction: Calling capital a relation does not deny it is made of things. It says machines or money function as capital only where they are owned by some and set in motion by others’ labour for the sake of valorization.

source.label: Section One: the production process of capital (p. 250)

furtherReading.label: Productive labour and labour as a service (p. 272)

quiz.question: Why does Marx reject defining capital as accumulated labour used in production?
options: It makes capital an eternal feature of all production, hiding its historical specificity
It overstates the role of labour
quiz.explanation: If any tool is capital, capitalism looks natural and timeless.

quiz.question: What use value must money-as-capital buy to grow?
quiz.explanation: Only living labour creates more value than it costs; objectified labour merely transfers value.

lessons.title: Labour as absolute poverty
lessons.description: The exchange between capital and labour splits into two different processes, and labour appears both as total exclusion from wealth and as its living source.
objectives: Name the two processes in the capital–labour exchange
Explain labour as ‘absolute poverty’ and ‘general possibility of wealth’
Note how ‘labour’ becomes ‘labour-power’ in Capital

sections.heading: Two different processes
paragraphs: In the first process, the worker sells a commodity—the disposal over his labour—for a definite sum of money. This is ordinary exchange: equivalent against equivalent, entirely within simple circulation.

In the second, the capitalist obtains labour itself as value-creating activity, the productive force that maintains and multiplies capital. This second process is qualitatively different from exchange; it happens in production, after the contract is signed.

sections.heading: Absolute poverty, general possibility
paragraphs: The precondition is a separation: labour stands apart from all means of production and subsistence. Labour without property is, in Marx’s phrase, absolute poverty—not a shortage, but complete exclusion from objective wealth.

Yet the same labour is the general possibility of wealth, as subject and activity. It confronts capital as labour in general, indifferent to any particular kind: the worker must be able to do whatever capital requires.
sections.callout: Nothing to sell but the ability to make everything.

sections.heading: Equivalents, savings, and loss
paragraphs: What the worker receives is money, the general form of wealth—but only as a means of subsistence that is spent and must be earned again. Marx mocks the economists’ advice that workers grow rich by saving: if all saved, wages would fall, and saving at best smooths the worker’s own fluctuations.
Meanwhile the creative power of labour passes to capital. The worker gives up that power for a fixed sum, the way Esau sold his birthright for a dish of food (p. 307).

example.title: A day’s pay and a day’s work
example.body: A firm pays a daily wage equal to what a worker needs to live. That transaction is fair by market rules. Then the worker spends the day producing goods worth more than the wage. The first step is exchange; the second is use.

lessons.distinction: The Grundrisse mostly says the worker sells ‘labour’ or ‘labour capacity’. Capital sharpens this to ‘labour-power’ to show how equal exchange coexists with surplus value. Read the earlier terms as a theory in formation, not a different theory.

source.label: Separation of labour and property; labour as absolute poverty (p. 295)

furtherReading.label: Two processes in the exchange of capital with labour (p. 274)

quiz.question: What are the two processes in the exchange of capital and labour?
options: Buying machines and buying raw materials
An exchange of equivalents for money, and the capitalist’s use of labour as value-creating activity
quiz.explanation: The wage bargain is ordinary exchange; the use of labour in production is a different kind of process.

quiz.question: Labour as ‘absolute poverty’ means…
options: labour is excluded from all objective wealth, yet is the general possibility of wealth
workers always earn less than subsistence
quiz.explanation: Propertyless labour has nothing but itself—which is also the source of all value.

lessons.title: Surplus value as surplus labour
lessons.description: The moment the theory of surplus value is born: the increment comes from labour time beyond what reproduces the worker—and this gives capital a historic, but transitory, role.
objectives: Explain surplus value as surplus labour time
Describe what Marx calls capital’s historic quality
Contrast Marx with the Physiocrats, Smith and Ricardo on the source of profit

sections.heading: Where the increment comes from
paragraphs: Capital must come out of production larger than it went in, yet every exchange it makes is an exchange of equivalents. The increase cannot come from circulation. It comes from time: if half a working day suffices to produce the worker’s means of life, the other half is surplus labour, and the value it creates is surplus value.

This is the first time Marx formulates the idea in a sustained way. Surplus value equals surplus labour time; the realization of capital (Verwertung) is the process in which living labour adds more value than it costs.

sections.heading: Capital’s historic quality
paragraphs: Surplus labour is older than capital—slaves and serfs performed it. What capital adds is an unlimited drive. It pushes labour beyond the limits of natural need, makes industriousness general, and develops productive forces to the point where surplus labour becomes a general need and much less labour suffices for society’s needs (p. 325).

Marx calls this the great historic quality of capital and, in the same breath, a historical and transitory one: once the productive forces have developed far enough, the compulsion to create surplus labour for capital loses its justification.
sections.callout: Capital makes humanity more productive than any previous order—and thereby makes its own form of compulsion questionable.

sections.heading: Reading the predecessors
paragraphs: The Physiocrats saw surplus only in agriculture, as a gift of the soil. Adam Smith glimpsed that profit is a deduction from the product of labour but wavered. Ricardo treated profit as an excess over wages yet never asked how an exchange of equivalents produces it; his focus was the distribution of a given product.
Marx’s step is to locate the source in the use of labour inside production and to treat distribution as following from it.

example.title: A bakery shift
example.body: An eight-hour shift. The bread baked in the first four hours sells for as much as the baker’s daily wage. The bread from the remaining four hours belongs to the owner without any equivalent being paid. Nothing was stolen at the counter; the surplus lies in the length of the day relative to the cost of the worker.

lessons.distinction: Surplus labour is not unique to capitalism. What is specific is its form: extracted through equal exchange, counted as value, and pursued without a natural limit.

furtherReading.label: Capital as creator of surplus labour (p. 325)

quiz.question: Where does surplus value come from in the Grundrisse’s account?
options: Labour time beyond what is needed to reproduce the worker
quiz.explanation: Equivalents are exchanged; the surplus lies in the extra time living labour works.

quiz.question: Why is capital’s creation of surplus labour ‘historic’ but ‘transitory’?
options: It develops productive forces and needs so far that its own compulsion can become unnecessary
quiz.explanation: Capital’s drive builds the productive capacity that could make capitalist surplus labour superfluous.

lessons.title: The arithmetic of productivity
lessons.description: Marx works through what happens to surplus value when productivity doubles—and finds each doubling adds proportionally less.
objectives: Calculate surplus labour after successive productivity doublings
State why gains in surplus value shrink
Connect relative surplus value to cheaper products and expanding output

sections.heading: Doubling productivity
paragraphs: Suppose necessary labour takes half the working day. If productivity doubles, the worker’s means of subsistence can be produced in a quarter of the day, so surplus labour rises from one half to three quarters. If productivity doubles again, necessary labour falls to an eighth and surplus labour to seven eighths.
This is relative surplus value: the working day stays the same length, but the share devoted to the worker’s own reproduction shrinks because the goods the worker consumes have become cheaper.

sections.heading: Smaller and smaller gains
paragraphs: The first doubling added a quarter of the day to surplus labour; the second added only an eighth; the third will add a sixteenth. The larger the surplus already is, the smaller the proportional increase each further rise in productivity can bring.

Necessary labour can never fall to zero, so the realization of capital becomes harder as productivity grows (p. 340). Yet each capital must keep raising productivity, under the pressure of competition.
sections.callout: Each doubling of productivity halves necessary labour—and adds only half as much surplus as the last.

sections.heading: Cheaper goods, more goods
paragraphs: Higher productivity lowers the value of each unit. To realize the larger surplus, capital must produce and sell more units, which pushes it toward new markets and new needs. The arithmetic here connects directly to the later passages on overproduction and devaluation.
Absolute surplus value lengthens the day; relative surplus value reshapes its division. The Grundrisse develops both, and Capital later organizes them into separate parts.

example.title: Run the numbers
example.body: Start at necessary labour = 1/2. Doubling 1: necessary 1/4, surplus 3/4 (+1/4). Doubling 2: necessary 1/8, surplus 7/8 (+1/8). Doubling 3: necessary 1/16, surplus 15/16 (+1/16). Open the Productivity lab to vary the starting point.

lessons.distinction: This is not a proof that capitalism must collapse. It shows a tendency for each productivity gain to add proportionally less surplus value; capital can offset it by lengthening or intensifying work, employing more workers, or cheapening means of production.

furtherReading.label: Realization grows harder as necessary labour falls (p. 340)

quiz.question: If necessary labour is 1/4 of the day and productivity doubles, surplus labour becomes…
quiz.explanation: Necessary labour falls to 1/8, so surplus labour is 7/8—a gain of only 1/8.

quiz.question: What general conclusion does Marx draw?
options: Each doubling adds the same surplus
The larger the existing surplus, the smaller the proportional gain from further productivity
Necessary labour can fall to zero
quiz.explanation: Halving an already small necessary share frees less additional time.

lessons.title: Living labour and the inversion of appropriation
lessons.description: Labour preserves old value for nothing, realizes itself as an alien power, and turns the law of property based on one’s own labour into its opposite.
objectives: Explain why preserving old value costs capital nothing
Describe realization as ‘de-realization’
State the inversion of the law of appropriation

sections.heading: Preserving value for free
paragraphs: Raw materials left alone decay and machines left idle rust. By using them as use values in work, living labour keeps their value alive and carries it into the new product. Marx stresses that this preservation is a free gift of living labour to capital: the capitalist pays for new labour, not for the preservation of old value (pp. 362–5).
The capitalist then claims a reward for allowing the worker to preserve the old capital—a claim Marx finds comic.

sections.heading: Realization as de-realization
paragraphs: The more the worker produces, the more the products confront him as someone else’s property—as capital, an alien power that employs him (p. 452). He leaves production as poor as he entered it, while the objective conditions of labour grow ever more powerful against him.
Here the theme of alienated labour from 1844 returns, now grounded in the theory of value and surplus value rather than in a philosophy of human essence alone.
sections.callout: Labour realizes itself—in a world that belongs to someone else.

sections.heading: The inversion of the law of appropriation
paragraphs: At first, property seems based on one’s own labour, and exchange swaps equivalents. But once capital consists of capitalized surplus value—surplus capital II—it buys new labour with the product of labour previously appropriated without equivalent (pp. 456–8).

The right of property turns into the right to appropriate others’ labour, and into the worker’s duty to treat the product of his own labour as another’s property. Nothing illegal has happened; every single exchange can be equal. The inversion is produced by the system working normally.

example.title: Year one and year ten
example.body: A firm may start with its founder’s savings. Ten years of reinvested profit later, nearly all of its capital consists of surplus value produced by past employees. The workers hired today are paid out of what yesterday’s workers produced unpaid.

lessons.distinction: The inversion is not fraud or a breach of contract. Its force comes precisely from occurring through equal exchanges; that is why Marx treats it as a law of the system rather than a moral failing of individuals.

source.label: Inversion of the law of appropriation (p. 458)

furtherReading.label: Labour preserves the value of material and instrument (p. 354)

quiz.question: Why is living labour’s preservation of old value ‘free’ for capital?
options: Using materials and tools as use values keeps their value alive without capital paying separately for it
quiz.explanation: Capital pays for new labour; the preservation of transferred value comes along with it.

quiz.question: The ‘inversion of the law of appropriation’ refers to…
options: property seemingly founded on one’s own labour becoming the right to appropriate others’ labour, through equal exchanges
the reversal of supply and demand
quiz.explanation: Capitalized surplus value buys new labour; ownership now rests on past unpaid labour.

lessons.title: Forms preceding capitalist production
lessons.description: The famous excursus on Asiatic, ancient and Germanic forms of property: how individuals once related to land as members of communities, and what had to dissolve for free labour to appear.
objectives: State the question the excursus answers
Compare the Asiatic, ancient and Germanic forms
Explain why these forms aimed at use value rather than wealth

sections.heading: The question
paragraphs: Capital presupposes free labour separated from its objective conditions—above all from land. The excursus asks how that separation came about by looking at forms in which it had not yet occurred: forms in which individuals relate to the land as their own, as members of a community.

In all of them, the community is the presupposition of property. One is an owner because one belongs, and the aim of labour is the reproduction of the individual within that community, not the accumulation of value.

sections.heading: Three forms of community
paragraphs: In the Asiatic form a comprehensive unity—often embodied in a despot—appears as the higher proprietor, while self-sustaining village communities combine agriculture and handicraft and are extremely stable. In the ancient (classical) form the city is the centre; land is split into public land and the private plots of citizens, and war is the community’s great common task. In the Germanic form, independent households live scattered, and the community exists chiefly when its members assemble.

Marx also discusses property in the instrument, as in the guild crafts, and forms like slavery and serfdom where the worker himself counts among the conditions of production. Capitalism requires the dissolution of all of these.

sections.heading: Wealth as the aim of production
paragraphs: The ancients asked which form of property produces the best citizens, never which is most productive. In the modern world, production is the aim of humanity and wealth the aim of production.

Marx then turns the comparison around: stripped of its narrow bourgeois form, what is wealth if not the universality of human needs, capacities and enjoyments—the full development of human powers as an end in itself? Seen this way the ancient world looks loftier, yet it offered only a limited satisfaction.
sections.callout: Before capital: the community was the premise of property. Under capital: the market is.

example.title: One field, three relations
example.body: A plot cultivated by a family belongs, in the Asiatic form, ultimately to the higher unity; in the ancient form to a citizen because he is a citizen; in the Germanic form to an independent household that meets its neighbours in assembly. In none of them is the farmer separated from the field.

lessons.distinction: The excursus relies on 1850s scholarship that has since been superseded, and the ‘Asiatic mode’ is especially contested. Read it as a theoretical typology of property and community, not as reliable history or ethnography. It became widely known through Hobsbawm’s 1964 edition, Pre-Capitalist Economic Formations.

furtherReading.label: Exchange of labour for labour rests on propertylessness (p. 514)

quiz.question: In the pre-capitalist forms, the individual relates to land…
options: as an anonymous buyer on a market
as a member of a community, which is the presupposition of ownership
quiz.explanation: Belonging to the community is what makes one an owner or possessor of land.

quiz.question: What distinguishes the Germanic form in Marx’s sketch?
options: A despotic unity owns all land
Independent households, with the community existing chiefly in periodic assembly
The city is the centre and public land is central
quiz.explanation: Germanic community is a union of independent landowners rather than a pre-existing unity.

lessons.title: Capital posits its own presuppositions
lessons.description: Historical origins versus present-day reproduction: once established, capital produces the very conditions it once needed from outside.
objectives: Distinguish historical from contemporary presuppositions of capital
Explain why money wealth alone could not create capital
Describe the double freedom of the wage labourer

sections.heading: History and present
paragraphs: Some conditions of capital—an accumulation of money, a mass of free labourers—belong to its prehistory. Once capital exists, it no longer needs to find these conditions; it produces them itself. Wages keep workers propertyless; profits accumulate new capital. Presuppositions have become results (pp. 459–61).
Marx compares this to an organic system that, as it develops into a totality, subordinates all elements of society to itself or creates the organs it still lacks.

sections.heading: Dissolution, not just accumulation
paragraphs: Merchant and money wealth existed for centuries without producing capitalism. It could buy labour and land only once older relations had dissolved: property in land, guild privileges, ties of clientship and service. Original accumulation is above all this dissolution.
The result is free labour in a double sense—free of personal bonds, and free of any means of production. Only then can money meet labour on the market as its counterpart.
sections.callout: Money did not create the propertyless worker; it found him, once the old ties had broken.

sections.heading: Where history must enter
paragraphs: Marx notes that his method shows the points at which historical investigation must come in. The dialectical presentation of capital points beyond itself to a past it presupposes but cannot deduce.
Capital Volume I later develops this into the account of ‘so-called primitive accumulation’: enclosures, colonial plunder, bloody legislation against vagrants.

example.title: A start-up and the first mill
example.body: A start-up today simply advertises a job: dispossessed workers already exist and its profits will help keep it so. The first cotton mills of the eighteenth century depended on enclosures, poor laws and the ruin of handicrafts to find hands at all.

lessons.distinction: Saying capital produces its presuppositions does not mean it created them originally. Its origins were violent and contingent; its reproduction is routine.

furtherReading.label: Capital I, Chapter 26: The secret of primitive accumulation

quiz.question: What does it mean that capital ‘posits its own presuppositions’?
options: Once established, capital reproduces conditions—like propertyless labour—that it historically required
quiz.explanation: Historical preconditions become ongoing results of capitalist production.

quiz.question: Why was money wealth alone insufficient to create capital?
options: Labour first had to be separated from its objective conditions by the dissolution of older relations
quiz.explanation: Money can buy labour only where people have been freed from land, guilds and personal ties.

lessons.title: The world market and capital’s civilizing influence
lessons.description: Relative surplus value requires new consumption; capital tears down every barrier—and meets its real limit in itself.
objectives: Explain why relative surplus value requires new needs and markets
Describe the ambivalent ‘civilizing influence’ of capital
Distinguish barriers from the limit capital is to itself

sections.heading: Expansion as necessity
paragraphs: More surplus labour means more products, which must be sold. Capital must therefore produce new consumption: enlarge existing consumption, spread needs to a wider circle, and create new needs by discovering new use values and exploring nature in every direction.
The tendency to create the world market is directly given in the concept of capital. Every limit appears to it as a barrier to be overcome.

sections.heading: The civilizing influence
paragraphs: Hence, Marx writes, the great civilizing influence of capital (p. 409): it drives beyond national barriers and prejudices, beyond the deification of nature, beyond traditional, self-satisfied ways of life. Earlier stages look like merely local developments by comparison.
The same movement makes nature purely an object for humankind, a matter of utility. The universalizing and the instrumentalizing sides arrive together.
sections.callout: Capital universalizes human needs—and reduces nature to a resource.

sections.heading: Barriers and the real limit
paragraphs: Capital overcomes barriers ideally, but they return. Its true limit is capital itself (pp. 415–22). It is the unity of production and realization, yet the two can separate: each capitalist treats his own workers as a cost to be cut and everyone else’s workers as consumers who should spend.
The result is overproduction relative to what can be sold at a profit, and the devaluation of capital in crises—a theme that runs from these pages to the crisis passages of Section Three.

example.title: Wanted: customers, not wages
example.body: A retailer wants low wages for its own staff and high incomes everywhere else. Each firm reasons the same way. Taken together, their wage policies restrict the demand all of them depend on.

lessons.distinction: ‘Civilizing’ is not praise of colonial conquest. Marx describes a contradictory process that destroys local forms and natural limits while universalizing needs; ecological and postcolonial readers have pressed hard on this passage.

source.label: Section Two: the circulation process of capital (p. 401)

furtherReading.label: Capital as unity and contradiction of production and realization (p. 414)

quiz.question: Why does relative surplus value require ‘the production of new consumption’?
options: Larger output must be sold, so capital must expand needs, markets and use values
quiz.explanation: Surplus value is realized only through sale, so capital must keep enlarging consumption.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a ‘barrier’ and capital’s ‘limit’?
options: Barriers are external obstacles capital drives past; its true limit is capital itself
Limits are legal; barriers are natural
quiz.explanation: Capital can surmount external obstacles; its own form of production for valorization keeps recreating them.

lessons.title: Circulation time and the annihilation of space
lessons.description: While capital circulates it does not valorize: circulation time is time of devaluation, and capital strives to annihilate space by time.
objectives: Explain why circulation time limits valorization
Calculate the effect of turnover on annual surplus value
Describe the drive to annihilate space by time

sections.heading: Time outside production
paragraphs: Capital passes through production and then through circulation—waiting as commodities to be sold, then as money to be laid out again. Only in production does it create value. Circulation time is therefore time of devaluation (p. 537): the longer it lasts, the fewer times a year capital can valorize itself.

Velocity substitutes for volume (p. 518). A smaller capital that turns over quickly can realize as much surplus value as a larger one that turns over slowly. Capital’s ideal is circulation without circulation time.

sections.heading: Annihilating space by time
paragraphs: Distance to markets lengthens circulation. Capital therefore strives to tear down every spatial barrier to exchange and conquer the whole earth as its market, and at the same time to annihilate space by time—to cut to a minimum the time spent moving from one place to another (p. 539).

Transport and communication become general conditions of production. Moving the product to market, Marx argues, belongs to the production process itself and can add value (p. 533), while pure circulation costs do not.
sections.callout: Railways, telegraphs, container ships, fibre optics: one long campaign against circulation time.

sections.heading: Credit and continuity
paragraphs: Credit bridges circulation time by anticipating future sales. And continuous production requires dividing capital so that some parts produce while others circulate (p. 548).
Later notebooks (pp. 650–68) work through production time, circulation time and turnover time in detail; they are the seed of Capital Volume II.

example.title: Fast fashion
example.body: Two clothing firms each advance the same capital. One needs four weeks to produce and eight to sell; the other two and two. The second turns its capital over three times as often and, at the same rate of surplus value, makes three times the annual surplus. Try it in the Circulation lab.

lessons.distinction: Circulation is not a source of value in Marx’s account, but neither is it neutral: it conditions how much value a given capital can valorize in a year.

source.label: Circulation time as time of devaluation (p. 537)

quiz.question: Why does Marx call circulation time ‘time of devaluation’?
options: While capital circulates it does not create surplus value, lowering its annual valorization
quiz.explanation: Fewer turnovers per year means less surplus value from the same capital.

quiz.question: What does ‘annihilating space by time’ mean?
options: Reducing the time needed to move goods and information across distance
quiz.explanation: Faster transport and communication shrink circulation time across space.

lessons.title: The Fragment on Machines
lessons.description: The most debated pages of the manuscript: the automatic system, the ‘general intellect’, capital as moving contradiction, and disposable time.
objectives: Describe the shift from tool to automatic system
Explain the ‘general intellect’
State why capital is a ‘moving contradiction’

sections.heading: From tool to automatic system
paragraphs: With the tool, the worker’s skill animates the instrument. In the automatic system of machinery the relation is reversed: the machine possesses the skill and strength, and the worker becomes a watchman and regulator alongside it.

The means of labour becomes fixed capital, and the knowledge built into it confronts the worker as an alien power—as the power of capital. The productive powers of labour are transposed into powers of capital (p. 699).

sections.heading: The general intellect
paragraphs: As large-scale industry develops, the creation of real wealth comes to depend less on labour time and the quantity of labour employed than on the power of the agencies set in motion—on science and its technological application.

Nature builds no machines, Marx writes; they are organs of the human brain created by the human hand, the power of knowledge objectified. Fixed capital shows how far general social knowledge has become a direct force of production—how far social life has come under the control of the ‘general intellect’ (p. 706; the phrase is in English in Marx’s German).

sections.heading: The moving contradiction
paragraphs: Capital presses to reduce labour time to a minimum while positing labour time as the sole measure and source of wealth (p. 706). As direct labour shrinks, labour time ceases to be the measure of wealth—and exchange value must cease to be the measure of use value.

Capital thereby creates disposable time, the true measure of wealth in a free society, but converts it into surplus labour (p. 708). The alternative Marx sketches is free time for all: time for the artistic, scientific and personal development of individuals, which in turn becomes the greatest productive force.
sections.callout: Capital calls science into life—and still insists wealth be counted in hours.

example.title: An automated warehouse
example.body: Robots and software multiply what each worker moves per hour. Labour hours shrink, yet income remains tied to hours worked, so workers compete for shifts while the machines could free time for everyone. Explore this in the Machines lab.

lessons.distinction: No passage is more contested. Negri and the post-operaist tradition read the Fragment as forecasting a knowledge economy beyond the law of value; Postone reads it as a critique of labour itself; critics such as Michael Heinrich note that Capital drops this ‘breakdown of the measure’ framing. Read it as a bold extrapolation, not a settled prediction.

source.label: Fixed capital; means of labour; machine (p. 690)

furtherReading.label: Value as measure versus development; disposable time (p. 704)

quiz.question: What does Marx mean by the ‘general intellect’?
options: The average skill of individual workers
Social knowledge and science that have become a direct force of production
quiz.explanation: Fixed capital objectifies general social knowledge as productive power.

quiz.question: Why is capital a ‘moving contradiction’?
options: It reduces labour time to a minimum while making labour time the sole measure and source of wealth
It alternates randomly between booms and busts
quiz.explanation: Automation undermines the very measure—labour time—on which capital’s wealth depends.

lessons.title: Falling profit and the afterlives of the Grundrisse
lessons.description: The ‘most important law’ of political economy, how the draft became Capital, and eighty years of competing readings.
objectives: Explain Marx’s argument for a falling rate of profit
Trace how the manuscript’s structure fed into Capital
Compare major readings of the Grundrisse

sections.heading: The most important law
paragraphs: In Section Three, capital appears as ‘fructiferous’: surplus value is measured against the whole capital advanced, as profit. Because fixed capital grows faster than the living labour that alone creates surplus value, the rate of profit tends to fall even while the rate of surplus value rises. Marx calls this in every respect the most important law of modern political economy (p. 748).

He links it to crises in which capital is destroyed and devalued, restoring the conditions for profit. Whether the tendency really holds, and what offsets it, remains one of the most argued questions in Marxian economics.

sections.heading: From draft to Capital
paragraphs: The last notebook opens a section headed Value, which Marx marked to be brought forward (p. 881). The commodity, not money, would become the starting point—as it is in the 1859 Contribution and in Capital.

The six-book plan of 1857–8 (capital, landed property, wage labour, the state, foreign trade, the world market) shrank over the next decade into the three volumes of Capital. The short critique of Bastiat and Carey, written in July 1857, shows the harmony economists Marx was arguing against from the start.

sections.heading: Afterlives
paragraphs: Roman Rosdolsky’s The Making of Marx’s ‘Capital’ (1968) used the Grundrisse to reconstruct Marx’s method and plan. Eric Hobsbawm’s 1964 edition of the pre-capitalist excursus shaped debates on historical materialism. Martin Nicolaus’s 1973 translation brought the whole text to English readers.

Antonio Negri’s Marx beyond Marx (1979) read the notebooks as the revolutionary core of Marx’s thought; Moishe Postone’s Time, Labor, and Social Domination (1993) as a critique of labour-time itself. More recently, debates on automation, platforms and AI have returned again and again to the Fragment on Machines—while other readers argue the Grundrisse is a more Hegelian draft that Capital corrected.
sections.callout: Every generation finds a different Grundrisse. Check each reading against the page.

example.title: Two readings of AI
example.body: One reader sees AI as the general intellect made literal—knowledge producing wealth with ever less labour, straining the law of value. Another replies that AI is fixed capital like any other: it transfers value, depends on cheap data and labour, and leaves the measure of wealth intact. Both cite pp. 704–6. Which reading fits the text better?

lessons.distinction: Reception history reveals the readers as much as the text. Keep apart what the Grundrisse says, what Capital later says, and what interpreters argue.

quiz.question: Why does the rate of profit tend to fall in Marx’s argument?
options: Wages always rise faster than prices
Total capital, especially fixed capital, grows faster than living labour, the sole source of surplus value
quiz.explanation: Surplus value is measured against an ever larger capital that labour does not grow as fast as.

quiz.question: Which work reads the Grundrisse as the revolutionary core of Marx’s thought?
quiz.explanation: Negri’s 1978 Paris lectures, published in 1979, made the Grundrisse central to post-operaist Marxism.

glossaryTerms.definition: Marx’s name for economic theories that start from an isolated individual producer, like Robinson Crusoe, as if that individual were natural rather than a product of modern society.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: The critique is not of thought experiments as such, but of treating a historical result as a timeless premise.

glossaryTerms.definition: An abstraction, such as ‘production in general’, that fixes features shared by all epochs and so avoids repetition.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: It becomes irrational when the common features are used to erase the specific difference of an epoch—e.g. to make capital eternal.

glossaryTerms.definition: A whole whose parts are internally related, so that each is defined through its relations to the others—as production, distribution, exchange and consumption are.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Totality does not mean all parts are equal: Marx says production predominates within it.

glossaryTerms.term: Rising from the abstract to the concrete
glossaryTerms.definition: Marx’s method of presentation: start from simple determinations and reconstruct the concrete as a ‘concentration of many determinations’.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: It describes how thought appropriates reality, not how reality comes into being—Marx’s point against Hegel.

glossaryTerms.definition: A dependent aspect of a process or whole, which has meaning only within it—like circulation as a moment of capital.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Not a ‘moment in time’. Read it as ‘aspect’ or ‘element in motion’.

glossaryTerms.definition: The non-mechanical relation between material production and other spheres, such as art or law, which may flourish or lag independently.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: It warns against reading culture off the economy one-to-one.

glossaryTerms.definition: Hegelian terms Marx uses for how a system makes its own starting conditions into results: capital ‘posits’ what it historically ‘presupposed’.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: To posit is to establish through the system’s own movement, not merely to assume.

glossaryTerms.definition: A proposed labour-money note certifying hours of work, advocated by Gray, Bray and Proudhonists as a replacement for gold.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Marx objects not to measuring time, but to the idea that money can be reformed while private exchange continues.

glossaryTerms.definition: The quantitative relation in which commodities exchange, which acquires an independent existence as money.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: In the Grundrisse ‘exchange value’ often still covers what Capital will separate into value and its form of appearance.

glossaryTerms.definition: The second great social form: individuals are personally independent but depend on impersonal relations such as prices and money.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: ‘Objective’ (sachlich) means thing-like and impersonal, not ‘unbiased’.

glossaryTerms.definition: The third social form Marx projects: universal development of individuals who control their common productivity as their own wealth.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: A possibility built on the second form, not a return to pre-modern community.

glossaryTerms.definition: The allocation and saving of social labour time, which Marx calls the first economic law even of communal production.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: It differs from value: time is planned directly instead of being validated afterwards through exchange.

glossaryTerms.definition: Money’s third function: as independent embodiment of wealth—treasure, means of payment, world money.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: It is not yet capital; it points toward capital because a hoard cannot grow by withdrawal.

glossaryTerms.definition: Money as the general substance of everyone’s survival, which replaces the communities it dissolves (Gemeinwesen).
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Marx uses ‘community’ ironically: a bond that stands over individuals as an external thing.

glossaryTerms.definition: The exchange of commodities and money (C–M–C) considered on its own, where exchangers appear as free and equal owners of equivalents.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Real but superficial: it presupposes processes outside circulation that it cannot explain.

glossaryTerms.definition: Value that preserves and increases itself through circulation by buying and using living labour; a historical social relation of production.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Not just tools or a sum of money: those are capital only in a specific social context.

glossaryTerms.definition: In the Grundrisse, labour exchanged against capital that produces capital—as opposed to services paid from revenue.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: It is a judgement about social form, not about usefulness or moral worth.

glossaryTerms.definition: The process by which capital preserves and increases its value in production; in Capital usually ‘valorization’.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Don’t confuse with realization in the sense of selling a product for money—Marx uses the word both ways.

glossaryTerms.definition: Labour time beyond what is necessary to reproduce the worker; under capital, the substance of surplus value.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Older than capitalism; what is new is its form as value and its limitless pursuit.

glossaryTerms.definition: Surplus value gained by reducing necessary labour time through higher productivity, with the working day unchanged.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Each productivity gain adds proportionally less surplus once necessary labour is already small.

glossaryTerms.definition: Surplus value reconverted into capital. ‘Surplus capital II’ is capital entirely formed from previously appropriated surplus labour.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: It is the key to the inversion of the law of appropriation.

glossaryTerms.term: Inversion of the law of appropriation
glossaryTerms.definition: The transformation of property based on one’s own labour into the right to appropriate others’ labour, achieved through equal exchanges.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: No exchange need be unfair for the inversion to occur.

glossaryTerms.definition: Arbeitsvermögen: the worker’s ability to labour, which Capital will call labour-power.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: The Grundrisse often says the worker sells ‘labour’; the terminology is still developing.

glossaryTerms.definition: Labour separated from all objective means of production and subsistence: total exclusion from wealth rather than a mere shortage.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: The same labour is also the general possibility of wealth.

glossaryTerms.definition: Labour as present activity, which creates new value and preserves old value, as opposed to objectified (past) labour in products.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Only living labour adds new value; means of production transfer theirs.

glossaryTerms.definition: The worker’s labour realizes itself in products that confront the worker as capital, an alien power.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: A value-theoretic restatement of the alienation theme from 1844.

glossaryTerms.definition: A form of property in which a comprehensive higher unity appears as proprietor and self-sustaining village communities are possessors.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Based on 1850s sources; heavily debated and not reliable ethnography.

glossaryTerms.definition: Classical form centred on the city: land divided into public land and citizens’ private plots, with war as the communal task.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Property here depends on citizenship.

glossaryTerms.definition: A form of property in which independent households live scattered and the community exists chiefly in assembly.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: The community is a union of owners, not a pre-existing unity.

glossaryTerms.definition: The historical process—above all a dissolution of older relations—that separated labour from its conditions and made capital possible.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Not saving by the thrifty, as the economists claimed. Capital calls it ‘so-called primitive accumulation’.

glossaryTerms.definition: Labour free in a double sense: free from personal bonds and free from (lacking) any means of production.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Both freedoms are necessary for a labour market.

glossaryTerms.definition: Capital’s drive to universalize needs, markets and knowledge, tearing down local barriers and traditional limits.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Descriptive and ambivalent—not an endorsement of conquest.

glossaryTerms.definition: A barrier is an obstacle capital strives to overcome; its true limit is capital itself—its form of production for valorization.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Overcoming barriers ideally does not abolish them in reality.

glossaryTerms.definition: Production beyond what can be sold at a profit, arising from the separation of production and realization.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Not too many goods for human needs, but too many for profitable sale.

glossaryTerms.definition: The time capital spends as commodities awaiting sale or money awaiting reinvestment, during which it creates no value.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Marx calls it time of devaluation; it lowers annual surplus value.

glossaryTerms.definition: The complete cycle of capital through production and circulation; the number of turnovers per year multiplies annual surplus value.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Velocity can substitute for volume of capital.

glossaryTerms.definition: Capital’s drive to shrink the time it takes to cross distances, through transport and communication.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: It does not abolish space; it reduces its cost in circulation time.

glossaryTerms.definition: Means of labour, above all machinery, whose value circulates only gradually; in the Fragment, the material form of social knowledge.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Fixed capital transfers value; the Fragment asks what happens when it, not labour, drives wealth creation.

glossaryTerms.definition: Marx’s English phrase for general social knowledge become a direct force of production, embodied in fixed capital.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Later writers extend it to living knowledge and cooperation; check what Marx himself ties it to.

glossaryTerms.definition: Capital reduces labour time to a minimum while positing labour time as the sole measure and source of wealth.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: A tension pushing the system, not a prediction of automatic collapse.

glossaryTerms.definition: Time freed from necessary labour, which capital converts into surplus labour but which could become free time for all.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Marx treats it as the true measure of wealth in a free society.

glossaryTerms.definition: The tendency for profit relative to total capital to decline as fixed capital grows faster than living labour.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: A tendency with counteracting factors, and still contested empirically and theoretically.

sourceParts.title: Introduction
sourceParts.subtitle: Production in general, the unity of production and consumption, and the method of rising from the abstract to the concrete.
sourceParts.editorialNote: Marx drafted this general introduction before starting the economic notebooks and then set it aside. In the 1859 Preface he explained that he had left it out because anticipating results not yet proven would confuse the reader. It is nonetheless the most widely read part of the manuscript.

sourceParts.title: The Chapter on Money
sourceParts.subtitle: A critique of Proudhonist bank reform that becomes a theory of money as measure, medium and independent form of wealth.
sourceParts.editorialNote: The chapter opens with statistics on the Bank of France and the reform proposals of Alfred Darimon, then turns into Marx’s first sustained theory of value and money. Much of it was reworked for the 1859 Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy.

sourceParts.editorialNote: The manuscript breaks off in notes. Its last notebook begins a section on Value, which Marx marked to be brought forward: the commodity would become the starting point of the 1859 Contribution and of Capital. The short critique of Bastiat and Carey was written in July 1857, before everything else.

companionTexts.title: A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy
companionTexts.description: The only part of the Grundrisse project Marx published himself: the commodity and money, with the famous Preface on base and superstructure.

companionTexts.title: Capital, Volume I
companionTexts.description: The finished presentation that grew out of these notebooks. Compare how commodity, money, labour-power and machinery are reorganized.

companionTexts.title: Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts
companionTexts.description: Marx’s first encounter with political economy and his theory of alienated labour, which the Grundrisse revisits on the ground of value theory.

companionTexts.title: The Poverty of Philosophy
companionTexts.description: Marx’s reply to Proudhon, the background to the Grundrisse’s attack on Darimon and labour-money schemes.

companionTexts.title: Wage Labour and Capital
companionTexts.description: Lectures to workers that state the capital–labour relation before Marx’s theory of surplus value was worked out.

companionTexts.title: Theories of Surplus Value
companionTexts.description: Marx’s long critical history of political economy, extending the reading notes on Ricardo, Smith and Malthus begun in the Grundrisse.
